This change is ready for review.

Why does it _need_ to contain timestamps?  Shouldn't the host OS have its own timestamps?

At a minimum this is going to need to be an option, I suspect.

We use this feature to monitor boot time in the fleet. Currently, this is not a requirement for any phase exit, but would be nice to have as early in NPI as possible to monitor the effect of different components and firmwares on boot time to be sure that we will be within our maintenance SLOs during production.

If the BIOS POST code is stuck (or looping), having a timestamp allows us to determine the exact time it occurred through the console log, providing more cross-reference points in terms of timing during debugging.

I think it would be a better approach to make all logs written by obmc-console have the same timestamp format.

This will make future maintenance easier. Based on current testing, special characters (such as colors, cursor movements, etc.) still retain their original formatting.

The serial console is not a stream of ASCII lines; it's essentially binary data, that *most of the time* is line-based.

What happens when a tui is started on the console? How are you intending to handle the tty control sequences? Inserting timestamps into that binary stream is going to make things messy...

What happens when a tui is started on the console? 
It will print the timestamp at the beginning and leave the rest unchanged.

How are you intending to handle the tty control sequences?
Control characters are still displayed in the same way as before, including colors, line breaks, cursor movements, and so on.

Indeed, if the input contains control characters like '\r', which moves the cursor back to the beginning of the line, using $cat to view the file may result in the timestamp being overwritten. However, if you open the file with $vi (which does not interpret control characters), the timestamp will be displayed correctly.

Hello. I wanted to chime into the discussion coming from bmcweb. Due to the fact, that the current redfish implementation for hostlogs coming from phosphor-hostlogger is unclear and there being an interest to move to the hostlogs coming from obmc-console, we would benefit from this change adding timestamps to the log messages.
How are you proposing to properly timestamp the box-drawing modes and cursor/screen control sequences?

The box-drawing mode is totally fine, because the entire box-drawing sequence is sent in one message, so there will be only a single timestamp before the drawing. I can show you what the log looks like if you want.

If the input contains control characters like '\r', which moves the cursor back to the beginning of the line, using "cat" to view the file may result in the timestamp being overwritten. However, if you open the file with "vi" (which does not interpret control characters), the timestamp will be displayed correctly.

> because the entire box-drawing sequence is sent in one message

you have no guarantee of that. you may be inserting a timestamp in the middle of a drawing sequence, or possibly as part of a terminal escape sequence.

There are multiple other scenarios where you cannot assume that you can insert text data into the serial output, expecting that it will be a valid "sentence" when parsed.

Still a no from me, as you're attempting to add timestamps to what is essentially a binary data stream.

What might work instead is a specific-text-only stream of the log data. This would be intended to use as an 8-bit-clean log of the data, and you would be able to timestamp/etc as necessary.

This would involve conversion from binary into ASCII (or even utf-8), before interpreting as text, and coming up with a strategy for that conversion. A simple initial approach may be to substitute invalid bytes.

So what you want is to keep the original binary log file as it is, and additionally create another log file by converting the binary data into text, adding timestamps on it.

In the end, there will be two log files, one is the original binary log generated by the existing flow, and the other is a text log that includes timestamps and has invalid bytes removed.

Is there anything wrong with my understanding?

Hi @patrick@stwcx.xyz, @andrew@codeconstruct.com.au, @joel@jms.id.au, @jk@ozlabs.org, @amithash@meta.com

Could you please help review this commits?

Thanks

This is the dependency commit:
https://gerrit.openbmc.org/c/openbmc/openbmc/+/82109

Could you please help review this commit?

Thanks

This seems verbose. Can we just call the config `log-timestamp`.
@andrew@codeconstruct.com.au what do you think? This would not impact default handling and we can enable it on a per-console basis. So, if there are binary transfers on particular consoles, it could be kept disabled there.
Sure, I will fix the config name.
Fix the config name from "is-enable-log-timestamp" to "log-timestamp".

I am not a user of the obmc-console log file, but in other context, I have found it dreadful to see my log file getting clobbered with timestamps. Those should really be part of the metadata/structured fields, like how you do structured logging in journald and defer displaying to another tool, journalctl.

I think we could do something similar here. Instead of storing the timestamp data directly in-band, _maybe_ you could probably store it side-band in an `xxx.log.timestamp` file instead, like a database index file.

Each line would store a pair of `timestamp len`, like

```
1762430400 0
1762430460 512
1762430520 1536
1762430580 2048
1762430640 2560
```

then have a display tool that grab the `xxx.log` and `xxx.log.timestamp`, use the timestamp and len to slice the log file and display the log in the time axis.

Bonus point:

- One that don't care about timestamp can still grab only the `xxx.log` file
- You can pipe the `xxx.log` file into some terminal emulator lib and get accurate boundaries between text and terminal control code, that would help not slicing the log file at awkward position that might break the output.

I have not thought of any reasons that this might not work.

>> You can pipe the xxx.log file into some terminal emulator lib and get accurate boundaries between text and terminal control code,

Thats a good use-case of maintaining a binary "pure" log file.

>> Each line would store a pair of timestamp len, like

Not liking this, since it would be a nightmare to maintain atomicity between the two files since they are both "rotated" at a fixed size. I would rather just duplicate the content into the .timestamp file.

> Not liking this, since it would be a nightmare to maintain atomicity between the two files since they are both "rotated" at a fixed size. I would rather just duplicate the content into the .timestamp file.

I am not sure what atomicity between two files mean (may be consistency?), but I don't see the reason why you cannot rotate them in lockstep :) When you need to rotate one, you also rotate the other, whether it is the log file or timestamp file. `xxx.log` and `xxx.log.1` has `xxx.log.timestamp` and `xxx.log.1.timestamp`. Am I missing something here?
Might be better if this was a member of `struct log_handler`.
Sure, i will fix it.

Why not just have generate_timestamp() taken in a buf and a len instead of returning a pointer to a static buf and copy it? It could return the number of bytes it added to the buf. I would probably wrap this all up in a function called init_log_sentence()
Sure, i will fix it.

@jk@ozlabs.org what do you think of a new config `logfile-timestamped = /path/to/text/file`. 
We will need a global config and a similar named section config for multiplexed consoles.

Yeah, I think it would be reasonable to create a separate text-friendly log stream for this. Whether that is timestamped or not could be configurable.

So maybe something like:

```
logfile-text = /path/to/text-log
logfile-text-timestamp = true
```

Conversion from the binary serial data to text-friendly is non-trivial though, we'd need to define the conversion policy there. Perhaps starting with just replacing non-ASCII characters may be sufficient? You'd still get the box-drawing characters (as they're just ASCII with a code switch), but that might be okay.

We could then do a more text-friendly log rotation too.
Sure, I’ll follow your approach and start by replacing non-ASCII characters as you suggested.

This change is ready for review.
